messages.subject: possible density plot
parts:
I am stumped by this.

First load the small dataset (117K)

load(url("http://www.biostat.jhsph.edu/~khansen/test.dat.rda"))

The code below produces two plots, which is viewable at
http://www.biostat.jhsph.edu/~khansen/ggplot_density.pdf

First a plot where the density estimation is extremely ragged,
essentially piecewise linear. I have 5 facets and 4 density estimates
per facet.

p <- ggplot(test.dat, aes(x = Chisq, Group = Weights, color = Dataset)) +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1), col = "grey60", alpha = 0.6) +
stat_density(geom = "path", position = "identity") +
facet_wrap( ~ Weights, ncol = 2) +
coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.2,2.2)) +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5,1, 1.5,2, 2.5, 3)) +
theme_grey(base_size = 8)
print(p)

Now, if I subset the data so instead of having 5 facets I only have 4,
I suddenly get much smoother (plot of) the density estimates. This
looks like a bug to me. The only difference is the data argument to
the ggplot function.

p <- ggplot(subset(test.dat, Weights != "1.2_21.26"), aes(x = Chisq,
Group = Weights, color = Dataset)) +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1), col = "grey60", alpha = 0.6) +
stat_density(geom = "path", position = "identity") +
facet_wrap( ~ Weights, ncol = 2) +
coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.2,2.2)) +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5,1, 1.5,2, 2.5, 3)) +
theme_grey(base_size = 8)
print(p)

The contents of the individual facets ought to be exactly the same,
but they are not. In general the density curves are also much less
smooth than what I get by plot(density(...)) (at least from a cursory
glance).

Also, I find it strange that I cannot specify bw to the stat_density
function (I am aware that this is documented).

Kasper

Thanks

This does help a lot, but I am still not really happy. If I do this,
I get the pdf at
http://www.biostat.jhsph.edu/~khansen/ggplot_density2.pdf

The first facet of the first plot is clearly "wrong". Granted, the
data in this facet is more extreme (outside of [0,2]) than the data in
the other facets, but it still has the majority of data in [0,2],
something you cannot tell based on the picture. How bad it is, is
easiest to see by selecting one of the flat lines in the facet and
doing a separate density estimate for this data. The result is the
last page of the pdf linked above, which clearly shows that the output
in the facet gives a completely wrong idea of what happens. So
somehow, what happens in the other facets, still affects the (plotting
of the) density estimates in the facet.

Kasper

Code:

load(url("http://www.biostat.jhsph.edu/~khansen/test.dat.rda"))
quartz(type = "pdf", file = "ggplot_density2.pdf")

p <- ggplot(test.dat, aes(x = Chisq, Group = Weights, color = Dataset)) +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1), col = "grey60", alpha = 0.6) +
stat_density(geom = "path", position = "identity") +
facet_wrap( ~ Weights, ncol = 2, scales = "free") +

coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.2,2.2)) +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5,1, 1.5,2, 2.5, 3)) +
theme_grey(base_size = 8)
print(p)
p <- ggplot(subset(test.dat, Weights != "1.2_21.26"), aes(x = Chisq,

Group = Weights, color = Dataset)) +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1), col = "grey60", alpha = 0.6) +

stat_density(geom = "path", position = "identity", bw = 0.00100) +
facet_wrap( ~ Weights, ncol = 2, scales = "free") +

coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.2,2.2)) +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5,1, 1.5,2, 2.5, 3)) +
theme_grey(base_size = 8)
print(p)

test2 <- subset(test.dat, Weights == "1.2_21.26" & Dataset == "WT")
plot(density(test2$Chisq), xlim = c(0,2))
dev.off()

messages.subject: Re: possible density plot
parts:
> First a plot where the density estimation is extremely ragged,
> essentially piecewise linear.  I have 5 facets and 4 density estimates
> per facet.
>
> p <- ggplot(test.dat, aes(x = Chisq, Group = Weights, color = Dataset)) +
>    geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 1), col = "grey60", alpha = 0.6) +
>    stat_density(geom = "path", position = "identity") +
>    facet_wrap( ~ Weights, ncol = 2) +
>    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.2,2.2)) +
>    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5,1, 1.5,2, 2.5, 3)) +
>    theme_grey(base_size = 8)
> print(p)

You are getting just what you asked for - coord_cartesian zooms into
just that region of the plot. When the range of the data is from 0 to
250 there's no point in calculating hundreds of density estimates in
the range 0 to 2. You want to change the limits of the scale, not
zoom in with the coordinate system.

Hadley

--

Department of Statistics / Rice University

those are the ones you are having problems with.

The algorithm I use to generate a grid of points on the x-axis is
crude, but I don't know of any better way to do it. To increase the
resolution of the density curve sufficient for it to be smooth in your
example would require 100s of additional points that most people would
never notice, but would make file sizes much larger and make plotting
even slower. If you can suggest a better way of picking points on the
x-axis, I'd be happy to consider it.

Hadley

I don't know how you do the density estimation, but if you use
base::density, it always returns 512 points (with default arguments).
So I would just use those 512 (x,y) values, instead of using an
equidistant grid (which is what I guess you do?)

Kasper

That is unfortunate.

I have been thinking a bit about this. If you use union(all
density$x) you get 512*n points giving rise to 512*n^2 lines. This
can quickly be big, but I would still suggest using the union of all
points. If not, I would suggest some subset of the union of points.
This may be what you use right now (or you may be using some grid on
union(range), I don't know for sure). But if it isn't I suggest
making it a subset of the union of the points.

Kasper
